> 需。有孚，光亨，貞吉。利涉大川。

需 is a common word in modern Chinese: to need.

In the 易 it does not mean that. And the difference is the whole hexagram.

## 需 is rain, and stopping

說文: 需，𩓣也。遇雨不進，止𩓣也。從雨，而聲.

Caught in rain, not advancing, waiting it out. The form carries 雨, and the oracle-bone shape shows a person with water on them.

The 彖 then glosses: 需，須也 — and 須 carries the sense of waiting.

So 需 is "to wait," not "to need."

The distance between the two is a distance between two postures. I need: reaching outward. I wait: holding inward. One of them cannot be done impatiently, and one cannot be done at all without impatience.

## 有孚 is not optimism

孚 is trustworthiness, solidity — the 易 uses it dozens of times, always as 信.

需's 有孚 is therefore not "believing the rain will stop." It is the state of being undeceitful and unagitated inside.

Because it is solid, it does not hurry. Because it does not hurry, it can wait.

That is the causal order in the text, and it runs from character to capacity, not from forecast to patience.

## 郊、沙、泥: a map

The first three lines place the waiting at three distances from danger:

郊 — open country, farthest from the peril.
沙 — the sand at the water's edge, closer.
泥 — mud at the bank, where the foot is already stuck.

Three characters, one map of approach. And the judgements reverse as the position advances: waiting far off is safe, waiting in the mud invites the thieves.

So the hexagram is not saying waiting is good. It is saying the same action changes its value with position.

## 血 and 穴

需於血，出自穴.

血 has two readings here: blood, the place of injury (Wang Bi: 凡稱血者，陰陽相傷者也), or 洫, a channel.

This book takes blood, because it pairs with 出自穴: one is in the midst of injury, the other comes out of the pit.

A pit is both where you hide and where you are trapped — and the line's movement is out.

## 不速之客 does not mean "unexpected guest"

速 here is not "fast." It is to summon — 儀禮 has 速賓, to call the guest.

不速 is: not summoned, and arrived anyway.

And 三人 is not a vague three people. Wang Bi is explicit: 三人，謂乾之三陽也 — the three yang lines of the lower trigram, which have finally come up.

Without that gloss, the top line is a stray anecdote. With it, it is the arrival the whole hexagram was waiting for.

## 需於酒食

酒食 is not festivity. In the archaic setting, a feast is sustenance and rest — 休養蓄養.

So the fifth line's waiting is not an empty interval. It is the interval in which the body is fed, which is what makes the later crossing possible.

## 利涉大川

And then the hexagram ends by crossing the great river.

The order is the point: wait, be fed, then cross. Not wait until you feel ready, and not cross because the waiting has become intolerable.

## A test

Name one thing you are currently calling a need. Then ask what it would look like as a wait: what you would do with the interval, and whether you would eat during it.
